A corps is a group of people who are formally organized together to carry out a specific role, function, or mission. The members of a corps share a common purpose, operate as a unified body, and usually work within some kind of structure or authority.

Think of it this way: if you gathered a random crowd, that's not a corps. But if you took a specific set of people, gave them a shared mission, organized them under leadership, and set them to work — that is a corps.
In the Military (the Most Common Use)

The word is used most heavily in military contexts. Here, a corps can mean two related things:

1. A large military unit

A corps is a specific level in the military hierarchy — larger than a division, smaller than a full army. It typically consists of two or more divisions and tens of thousands of soldiers. For example, during World War II, armies were broken into corps, which were broken into divisions, which were broken into regiments, and so on.

Example: "The III Corps was tasked with advancing through the northern flank."

2. A branch or service group within a military

Here, a corps refers to a specialized, named body of military personnel who perform a particular function. This is the sense you see in famous names:

  • The Marine Corps — the branch of the U.S. military specializing in amphibious operations and rapid deployment. All its members are Marines, and together they form this corps.
  • The Army Corps of Engineers — a specialized body of soldiers and civilians within the U.S. Army whose job is engineering: building bridges, managing waterways, constructing infrastructure.
  • The Medical Corps — military doctors, nurses, and medics organized as a distinct body within a larger armed force.

In this sense, a corps is essentially a professional community within a military — united by specialty, training, and identity.

The word extends naturally to civilian and professional life, wherever a defined group of people share a formal role or function:

  • The diplomatic corps — all the ambassadors and diplomats from foreign countries stationed in a particular nation, treated collectively as a body. When a country expels "the diplomatic corps," it means all foreign diplomats, not just one.
  • The press corps — the group of journalists assigned to cover a specific institution or beat. The White House press corps, for example, is the body of reporters whose job is specifically to cover the U.S. President and the White House.
  • The Peace Corps — a U.S. government organization in which volunteers go abroad to help communities in developing countries. Its members, taken together, form this corps.
  • The corps de ballet — in ballet, this refers to the ensemble of dancers who perform together as a group (as opposed to the principal soloists). They are the "body" of the ballet company.
  • A cadet corps — a group of young people organized for military-style training and discipline, often in schools or youth programs.

Across all these uses, notice what stays constant:

  1. It's always a group — never one person.
  2. The group is formally organized — not a casual gathering.
  3. They share a defined function or identity — soldiers of a particular type, journalists of a particular beat, diplomats of a particular posting, dancers of a particular role.
  4. They operate as a single, recognized body — a corps is addressed and treated as a unit.

So while words like team or crew suggest informal collaboration, corps carries a stronger sense of institutional identity, formal structure, and collective purpose. A corps has a kind of professional solidarity to it.

Because the word looks and sounds similar to other words, it's worth being precise:

  • It has nothing to do with a corporation (a business company). People sometimes write "corp" as a short form of corporation, but that is a completely different word and concept.
  • It has nothing to do with a corpse (a dead body). Despite the visual similarity, the two words are unrelated in meaning.

Corps = a formally organized body of people united by a shared purpose, role, or function.

It's used most often in military contexts — referring either to a large tactical unit or to a named branch of specialists — but it applies equally well to journalists, diplomats, volunteers, dancers, or any other group that is organized, defined, and functions as a unified body with a clear collective identity.
